newsitem.title: UK: European banks launch secondary loan association.
newsitem.headline: European banks launch secondary loan association.

text.p: A group of banks on Thursday confirmed they are to launch a European loan trading association aimed at increasing trading and developing the secondary market.

The Loan Market Association (LMA) is being launched by BZW, Credit Suisse, Fuji Bank, HSBC Investment Bank, JP Morgan, NatWest Markets and SBC Warburg. An LMA spokesman told Reuters a broad range of other institutions will be invited to join.
The LMA aims to "create greater liquidity in the loan market through the development of more active and efficient secondary market" and a more open and structured trading framework.

The group's initial focus will be on par loan trading -- loans which are valued near to the price at which they were issued, harnessing an already active market by creating standard settlement and operational procedures.

The LMA said it also plans to establish mechanisms to value such loans and help develop standard documentation for trading. It also aims to set up codes of practice for activity in a market which until now has developed on an ad-hoc basis.
The plans are not limited to loans to British companies and the scheme aims to encompass European markets.

The spokesman for the association said it would enable banks to free-up capital for further loans or other purposes and also enable them to manage loan portfolios more actively, minimising risk and increasing shareholder value.

He said the initial investor base would be largely banks. "We view this as largely a bank market, at least in the initial stages...other investors will come into this market as it becomes more of an asset class as a whole," he said.
The proposals had met with an enthusiastic response from other trading banks and loan arrangers in the market and the LMA was confident others will be quick to join, he added.

The LMA prospectus said that increased loan trading would benefit borrowers by increasing primary market liquidity, thereby improving pricing to the borrower and smoothing the sort of cyclical squeezes on liquidity seen in the past.
It said it will eventually broaden its reach to include "impaired value loan assets" -- loans that are trading at a substantial discount to face value.
A similar body, the Loan Syndication and Trading Association (LSTA), already operates in the U.S. That group was set up at the beginning of 1996 and already has around 55 members.
